# A disjoint-residual criterion for all-zero endpoint cap covers

This is a conditional geometric criterion, not a proof for arbitrary
three-fiber bodies. In particular the required section containment does
not follow from mere scalar supporting-facet capacities. The planar
centered-chord corollary retains its explicit additional premise.

Write Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d for d>=1. Ordinary d-dimensional volume is
denoted by vertical bars. The ordinary Grünbaum theorem is used in
its standard form: the centroid of a convex body L belongs to L and
every containing closed halfspace captures at least Gamma_d|L|.

## 1. An elementary positive-part cover bound

If a d-dimensional convex body L is covered by finitely many closed
halfspaces H_1,...,H_m, then for every alpha>=0,

    |L| <= sum_i (|L intersect H_i|-alpha)_+
                            + alpha/Gamma_d.          (1)

Here each halfspace has a nonzero normal. To prove the statement,
start with L_0=L and visit the halfspaces in order. If the current
mass c_i=|L_(i-1) intersect H_i| is at most alpha, keep the current
body. Otherwise slide the boundary of H_i toward its captured side
until the deeper cap has volume c_i-alpha, and remove that deeper
cap's interior by retaining the opposite closed halfspace. Such a
threshold exists by continuity of cap volume: in a full-dimensional
body the boundary hyperplane has zero d-volume, and thresholds vary
from mass c_i to zero. The retained set remains compact and convex,
and its mass in the original H_i is alpha. If a zero-volume retained
set occurs, (1) already follows from the removal bound below and the
argument stops. Otherwise it is again a convex body.

The removal at step i is at most (|L intersect H_i|-alpha)_+.
Later cuts do not increase any earlier halfspace mass. Therefore the
final convex body L' has volume at least

    |L|-sum_i (|L intersect H_i|-alpha)_+

and every H_i captures at most alpha of L'. Its centroid belongs to
one of the H_i because they cover L. Ordinary Grünbaum then gives
Gamma_d|L'|<=alpha, proving (1). The argument also covers alpha=0:
if every retained body had positive volume, its centroid would give
a positive captured mass, a contradiction.

This is the Gamma_d specialization of the stronger audited effective
cap-count theorem elsewhere in the workspace. Its short proof here
makes the particular dependency used below explicit.

## 2. Disjoint residuals give a mixed cap lower bound

Let A,K,B be d-dimensional convex bodies at integer bases -1,0,1,
where d>=1. Suppose a family of m>=2 ambient closed halfspaces has
middle traces covering K. Require that each cap has a nonzero continuous
normal. Assume each captures zero volume from B,
each captures at most Q total volume from the three fibers, and the
strict uncaptured parts R_i of A are pairwise disjoint up to measure
zero. Then

    Q >= Gamma_d (|A|+|K|).                           (2)

This implication itself requires neither midpoint compatibility nor
criticality; those geometric hypotheses are ways of seeking its stated
conditions in an actual problem.

Put a=|A|, k=|K|, r_i=|R_i|, and q_i=|K intersect H_i|. By definition
R_i is exactly the complement of the captured portion within A, so

    q_i+a-r_i <= Q,       sum_i r_i<=a.               (3)

If Q>=a, set alpha=Q-a in (1). By (3),

    (q_i-alpha)_+ <= r_i,
    k <= a+(Q-a)/Gamma_d.

Thus Q>=Gamma_d k+(1-Gamma_d)a>=Gamma_d(k+a), because
Gamma_d<=1/2 for all d>=1.

If Q<a, the elementary cover bound k<=sum q_i and (3) give

    k <= mQ-(m-1)a.

The strict inequality Q<a forces k<a, and consequently

    Q >= [k+(m-1)a]/m >= (k+a)/2 >= Gamma_d(k+a).

The middle inequality is equivalent to (m-2)(a-k)>=0. This proves
(2) in all cases, without interchanging a maximum and an infimum.

If the actual three-fiber mass is M=a+k+b and b=|B|<=a+k, (2) gives
Q>=Gamma_d M/2. If b>a+k, the ordinary centroid of the B fiber,
which is an actual mixed-integer point, already has raw mixed depth
at least Gamma_d b>Gamma_d M/2. Thus a putative sub-OC critical cover
cannot have the disjoint-residual property.

## 3. A common-simplex section containment forces disjointness

Let d>=2 and let v_1,...,v_(d+1) span R^d with sum v_i=0 and form
a minimal positive circuit. Write

    T={x: v_i.x<=1 for every i},
    -T={x: v_i.x>=-1 for every i}.

Let A be a convex body for which every cut v_i.x=-1 is proper.
Suppose the entire cutting section satisfies

    A intersect {v_i.x=-1} subset -T                 (4)

for every i. Then the open residual regions

    R_i=A intersect {v_i.x<-1}

are pairwise disjoint.

Suppose instead that some point belongs to R_i intersect R_j. Since
the inequalities are strict and A is full-dimensional, a small convex
mixture with an interior point produces a point p in int A still
satisfying both inequalities. Properness of cut i gives a nonempty
open set of points q in int A with v_i.q>-1. Choose q in that open
set so that the segment from p does not cross the two planes
v_i.x=-1 and v_j.x=-1 simultaneously. This exceptional simultaneity
condition is one affine hyperplane in q: the two normals are linearly
independent in a minimal positive circuit of dimension at least two.
The open set is therefore not contained in it.

The first exit of the segment from the two-inequality region crosses
one of those cutting planes while strictly violating the other
inequality. The crossing point is in A and outside -T. It contradicts
(4) for that cutting section. This proves disjointness. In d=1 the
analogous two residuals are automatically disjoint because their
normals are opposite; no generic segment argument is needed.

## 4. A precise planar centered-chord application

Consider actual full planar fibers A,K,B at -1,0,1 with
(A+B)/2 subset K and source y in int K. Suppose three depth-critical
caps through (0,y) have continuous normals forming a full-rank minimal
positive circuit. Assume all three B captures are zero and all three
A cuts are proper. Apply the allowed shear from Section 4 of
`candidate 568f7cf028ec23b6`
to put y=0 and the caps in the form v_i.x>=z, with sum v_i=0.

Impose the additional condition that every middle cutting chord has
centroid exactly 0. The planar moment-body lemma in
`candidate 6ac02348e3ceb9a9`
then gives the actual segment inclusion

    -(A intersect {v_i.x=-1})
                      subset B intersect {v_i.x=1} subset T.

Indeed the general inclusion is the reflected A segment translated
by minus the middle-to-A chord-length ratio times the middle chord
centroid, so the translation vanishes under the stated condition.
Consequently (4) holds, the A residuals are disjoint, and (2) applies
to the common critical mass Q. The middle traces cover K because
sum v_i=0 implies at least one v_i.x>=0 at every x.

If B is nonheavy, the source (0,y) itself has the OC guarantee. If B
is heavy, its ordinary centroid has that guarantee. All containing
ambient halfspaces are controlled in the first case because the caps
were genuinely depth-critical, not merely selected candidates of small
mass. The full statement for arbitrary middle-chord centroid shifts
has not been established; the quantitative chord-ratio bound alone
does not imply (4).

## 5. The larger residual budget that the argument actually permits

For a family of m caps with m>=1/Gamma_d, pairwise disjointness in
Section 2 can be replaced by the weaker numerical condition

    sum_i |R_i| <= (1/Gamma_d-1)|A|.                 (5)

In particular m=d+1 always meets the stated count condition, and in
dimension two the permitted total residual mass is 5|A|/4.

For completeness put kappa=(sum r_i)/a. If Q>=a, the same trimming
argument gives

    Q >= Gamma_d k+(1-Gamma_d*kappa)a
       >= Gamma_d(k+a).

If Q<a, the cover sum gives

    Q >= [k+(m-kappa)a]/m,      k<kappa*a.

Here kappa<=1/Gamma_d-1<=m-1. The function
(x+m-kappa)/(m(x+1)) is nonincreasing for x>=0, because its
derivative has the sign of kappa-(m-1). At x=k/a<kappa it is
therefore at least its value at kappa, namely 1/(1+kappa), which
is at least Gamma_d. This again proves (2). If kappa=0, the case
Q<a is impossible because k>0.

The elementary inequality Gamma_d>=1/(d+1) used for m=d+1 follows
from d^d>=(d+1)^(d-1); equivalently (1+1/d)^(d-1)<=d. For d=1
it is equality, for d=2 it is 3/2<=2, and for d>=3 the left side
is less than e<3<=d. Thus no asymptotic loss enters (5).

Condition (5) is a target for actual geometry, not a consequence
established here from supporting-facet capacities, chord-centroid
bounds, or no-heavy-fiber assumptions. The section-containment regime
of Section 3 proves the stronger sum r_i<=a and is a verified instance.
